{{Short description|Problem in topology}}

In [[point-set topology]], '''Kuratowski's closure-complement problem''' asks for the largest number of distinct sets obtainable by repeatedly applying the set operations of [[closure (topology)|closure]] and [[complement (set theory)|complement]] to a given starting subset of a [[topological space]].  The answer is 14.  This result was first published by [[Kazimierz Kuratowski]] in 1922.<ref>{{Cite journal
  | last = Kuratowski
  | first = Kazimierz
  | authorlink = Kazimierz Kuratowski
  | title = Sur l'operation A de l'Analysis Situs
  | url = http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm3/fm3121.pdf
  | journal = Fundamenta Mathematicae
  | volume = 3
  | pages = 182–199
  | publisher = Polish Academy of Sciences
  | location = Warsaw
  | year = 1922
  | doi = 10.4064/fm-3-1-182-199
 | issn = 0016-2736}}</ref> It gained additional exposure in Kuratowski's fundamental monograph ''Topologie'' (first published in French in 1933; the first English translation appeared in 1966) before achieving fame as a textbook exercise in [[John L. Kelley]]'s 1955 classic, ''General Topology''.<ref>{{Cite book
  | last = Kelley
  | first = John
  | isbn = 0-387-90125-6
  | authorlink = John L. Kelley
  | title = General Topology
  | publisher = Van Nostrand
  | year = 1955
  | page = 57}}</ref>

==Proof==
Letting <math>S</math> denote an arbitrary subset of a topological space, write <math>kS</math> for the closure of <math>S</math>, and <math>cS</math> for the complement of <math>S</math>. The following three identities imply that no more than 14 distinct sets are obtainable:

# <math>kkS=kS</math>. (The closure operation is [[idempotency|idempotent]].)
# <math>ccS=S</math>. (The complement operation is an [[involution (mathematics)|involution]].)
# <math>kckckckcS=kckcS</math>. (Or equivalently <math>kckckckS=kckckckccS=kckS</math>, using identity (2)).

The first two are trivial.  The third follows from the identity <math>kikiS=kiS</math> where <math>iS</math> is the [[interior (topology)|interior]] of <math>S</math> which is equal to the complement of the closure of the complement of <math>S</math>, <math>iS=ckcS</math>. (The operation <math>ki=kckc</math> is idempotent.)

A subset realizing the maximum of 14 is called a '''14-set'''.  The space of [[real numbers]] under the usual topology contains 14-sets.  Here is one example:
:<math>(0,1)\cup(1,2)\cup\{3\}\cup\bigl([4,5]\cap\Q\bigr),</math>
where <math>(1,2)</math> denotes an [[Interval (mathematics)#Definitions|open interval]] and <math>[4,5]</math> denotes a closed interval. Let <math>X</math> denote this set. Then the following 14 sets are accessible:

# <math>X</math>, the set shown above.
# <math>cX=(-\infty,0]\cup\{1\}\cup[2,3)\cup(3,4)\cup\bigl((4,5)\setminus\Q\bigr)\cup(5,\infty)</math>
# <math>kcX=(-\infty,0]\cup\{1\}\cup[2,\infty)</math>
# <math>ckcX=(0,1)\cup(1,2)</math>
# <math>kckcX=[0,2]</math>
# <math>ckckcX=(-\infty,0)\cup(2,\infty)</math>
# <math>kckckcX=(-\infty,0]\cup[2,\infty)</math>
# <math>ckckckcX=(0,2)</math>
# <math>kX=[0,2]\cup\{3\}\cup[4,5]</math>
# <math>ckX=(-\infty,0)\cup(2,3)\cup(3,4)\cup(5,\infty)</math>
# <math>kckX=(-\infty,0]\cup[2,4]\cup[5,\infty)</math>
# <math>ckckX=(0,2)\cup(4,5)</math>
# <math>kckckX=[0,2]\cup[4,5]</math>
# <math>ckckckX=(-\infty,0)\cup(2,4)\cup(5,\infty)</math>

==Further results==
Despite its origin within the context of a topological space, Kuratowski's closure-complement problem is actually more [[algebra]]ic than topological.  A surprising abundance of closely related problems and results have appeared since 1960, many of which have little or nothing to do with point-set topology.<ref>{{Cite journal
  | last = Hammer
  | first = P. C.
  | title = Kuratowski's Closure Theorem
  | journal = Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde
  | volume = 8
  | publisher = Royal Dutch Mathematical Society
  | pages = 74–80
  | year = 1960
  | issn = 0028-9825}}</ref>

Regarded as set-valued set functions, the 14 closure-complement operations comprise an [[Monoid#Acts_and_operator_monoids|operator monoid]] called the '''Kuratowski monoid''' where the monoid product is [[function composition]].<ref>{{Cite journal
  | last1 = Gardner
  | first1 = B. J.
  | last2 = Jackson
  | first2 = M.
  | title = The Kuratowski closure-complement theorem
  | journal = New Zealand Journal of Mathematics
  | volume = 38
  | publisher = New Zealand Mathematical Society
  | pages = 9–44
  | year = 2008
  | url = https://figshare.utas.edu.au/articles/journal_contribution/The_Kuratowski_Closure-Complement_Theorem/22870025/1/files/40607546.pdf
  | s2cid=11278456 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal
  | last = Bowron
  | first = Mark
  | title = Boundary-border extensions of the Kuratowski monoid
  | journal = Topology and its Applications
  | volume = 341
  | number = 108703
  | publisher = Elsevier
  | pages = 1–35
  | year = 2024
  | doi = 10.1016/j.topol.2023.108703
  | s2cid=257505589 | doi-access = free
  }}</ref>
This monoid, which can be used to classify topological spaces based on the [[quotient monoid|quotient]] they satisfy, has inspired similar classifications in other settings as well.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The radical-annihilator monoid of a ring|first=Ryan|last=Schwiebert|journal=Communications in Algebra |year=2017 |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=1601–1617 |doi=10.1080/00927872.2016.1222401|arxiv=1803.00516|s2cid=73715295 }}</ref>
